findings.location: lesson.json /prose/11/text in source and both modern editions; p0299#5
findings.title: Restore or explicitly account for the quantum-specific Vavilov result
findings.source_claim: The source reports that Vavilov's experiments established discrimination between illuminations differing by a small number of light quanta.
findings.observed: Chinese now says that he studied weak-light sensitivity and that small energy exchanges can produce visual effects. English likewise says he studied sensitivity and that small transfers can produce measurable effects. Neither preserves the reported small-number discrimination result.
findings.impact: The named example no longer supplies its source's specific connection between visual sensitivity and light quanta. Matching source_text fields and an adaptation audit pass do not repair that semantic omission.
findings.required_resolution: Preserve the result as an attributed historical report with its experimental/observer limitations, or explicitly record and justify its omission as a scientific adaptation. Do not convert it into a universal claim that every single photon is consciously visible.
findings.does_not_block: The independently checked photon energy, momentum, rest-mass qualification, or green-photon erratum.

findings.location: lesson.json /prose/3/text and /prose/4/text in both modern editions; p0296#6+p0297#1 and p0297#2
findings.title: Make the nonrelativistic scope of the speed form explicit
findings.observed: Equation (10.2) uses mv^2/2 without explicitly stating the low-electron-speed approximation. The surrounding text correctly treats maximum energy/speed and the single-photon regime.
findings.impact: The relation is appropriate for the ordinary optical/UV photoelectric setting, but mv^2/2 must not be read as an exact kinetic-energy expression for arbitrarily energetic photoelectrons.
findings.recommended_resolution: Explicitly identify m as electron mass and v as the maximum emitted speed in the nonrelativistic approximation; retain h*nu=A+K_max as the general energy-balance statement.

Printed decimal constants are understood as approximations, not exact identities to current SI values.
